newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Bangladesh signs nuke treaty; India, Pakistan don't.
newsitem.headline: Bangladesh signs nuke treaty; India, Pakistan don't.

text.p: Prime Minister Sheikhh Hasina on Thursday signed the nuclear test ban treaty on behalf of Bangladesh, one of 44 nations whose approval is necessary before the pact comes into force.

The treaty now has signatures from 129 states since it was opened for signing on Sept. 24. But before it takes effect, 44 nations with nuclear power, which include Bangladesh, are required to sign and then ratify it through their national legislatures.
With Bangladesh's signature, only three Asian countries -- India, Pakistan and North Korea -- remain among the 44 states that have not signed.

India has vowed never to sign "this unequal treaty" until the declared atomic powers -- the United States, Russia, Britain, France and China -- devise a timetable for destroying their nuclear arsenals. And Pakistan has said it would not sign until India does.
Hasina signed the document shortly after an address to the General Assembly where she spoke mainly about trade and development as well as migration that she said merited an international conference.

"Cogent arguments are often put forward in favour of unrestricted global flows of capital, trade and services," she said. "It seems to us that an equally persuasive case can be made for more deregulated movements of labour."

On nuclear weapons, she did not mention the test ban treaty but said the world was more than ready for nuclear disarmament. Atomic weapons are "an abomination and surely can have no place in a civilised world," she added,
Currently, the United States and Russia each deploy more than 7,000 warheads, France 512, Britain 464 and China 284.

The 41 states with a nuclear potential that have signed the test ban treaty, including the five nuclear powers, are Algeria, Argentina, Australia, Austria, Bangladesh, Belgium, Brazil, Bulgaria, Canada, Chile, Colombia, Egypt, Finland, Germany, Hungary, Indonesia, Iran, Israel, Italy, Japan, Mexico, Netherlands, Norway, Peru, Poland, Romania, Slovakia, South Korea, South Africa, Spain, Sweden, Switzerland, Turkey, Ukraine, Vietnam and Zaire.

U.S. President Bill Clinton, followed by the other declared nuclear powers, signed the Comprehensive Test Ban Treaty (CTBT) on Sept. 24 . Clinton said signature of the pact was tantamount to a ban on testing "even before the treaty formally enters into force."
The treaty requires a conference in three to four years for members to decide how to speed up the ratification process should India and others still refuse to join the pact.

Fiji is the only state so far to have ratified the treaty, which bans all explosions in the environment, whether in the atmosphere, space or underground, regardless of size. A 1963 treaty barred explosions in the atmosphere and another one in 1974 set a size limit on underground tests.
